120.title: Remembrance with breath
120.hook: simran is remembering the Name; here we let the breath carry it
120.howItsDone: Sikhs practice naam simran by repeating and meditating on the Name, often Waheguru, both in the early morning hours called amrit vela and in short moments throughout the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a small langar at home, feeding one person with no agenda. Your line was a small langar. Who's coming to your table? Day one hundred twenty.
screen: `A SMALL LANGAR AT HOME — A SMALL LANGAR.`

segments.voice: Think of what you carry everywhere without trying. Keys, most days. A phone, almost always. A worry or two. Every one of them has been left behind somewhere at least once: on a counter, in a cab, in a coat pocket. Except one. Your breath has never stayed home. It goes with you to the office, into the car, into a hospital bed, into sleep. It doesn't need a gurdwara or a book or a quiet room. On day seven of this path, simran was one of your first words, with the line remember on the inhale. Now, a hundred and thirteen days later, the path comes back to it, slowly, for a whole week.
screen: `THE ONE THING YOU NEVER LEAVE BEHIND.` →`IT GOES WITH YOU EVERYWHERE.` → `BACK TO SIMRAN.`

segments.voice: Naam simran. Naam is the Name: not just a word for God, but God's presence, the truth the Name points to. Simran is remembering, from an old word meaning to call to mind. Remembering the Name. It's the third pillar you met on day eleven, naam japna, and Sikhs call it the heart of the whole path. Seva gets the hands ready. Kirtan gets the voice and the ear ready. Simran is where it all turns inward. Guru Arjan opens the Sukhmani, the hymn of peace, with it. In paraphrase: remember, keep on remembering, and find peace; the troubles of the body and the mind will leave. And again and again the Guru Granth Sahib pairs remembering with breathing. The Gurus speak of remembering God with every breath and every bite, so that no breath goes by empty. That's why this week joins simran to the breath. The breath is always there, so the remembering can always be there. It's slow, so it slows the mind. And it's honest: you can't breathe yesterday or tomorrow, only now. Some Sikhs sit for long hours of simran before dawn, in the time the Gurus called amrit vela, the ambrosial hours. Others remember in short moments through the day: at a red light, in a waiting room, before picking up the phone. Both are simran. Today there's no technique yet. No special words. Just the breath, going in and out, and the Name held gently alongside it, however you understand it. Tomorrow, a way to give each breath its word.
screen: `NAAM AND SIMRAN.` · `THE THIRD PILLAR, TURNED INWARD.` · `REMEMBER, AND FIND PEACE.` · `WITH EVERY BREATH.` · then, large: `BREATH AND NAME.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, with your back upright and your hands resting. Close your eyes, or let them go soft. Don't change your breath yet. Just notice it: in, and out. Now let it slow down a little, longer on the way in, longer on the way out. Don't force anything. With each breath, let the Name be there in the background, the way a candle is there in a room. When your mind wanders, and it will, just come back to the next breath. The bell holds the time.
Naam simran. Remembering the Name: the heart of Sikh practice, and this week, carried on the breath.
Your line: breath and name. Today, three times, stop and take one slow breath with the Name held alongside it. Day one hundred twenty.

121.title: Wahe in, guru out
121.hook: many sound Wahe on the in-breath and Guru on the out-breath
121.howItsDone: Many Sikhs practice simran by silently sounding Wahe on the in-breath and Guru on the out-breath; others repeat Waheguru aloud or sing it together in kirtan.

segments.voice: Yesterday, naam simran, remembering the Name, and letting the breath carry it. Your line was breath and name. Did you notice your breathing even once after the lesson? Day one hundred twenty-one.

Breathing is the one thing you do all day without ever deciding to, and almost none of those breaths get noticed. The in-breath comes, the out-breath goes, and the whole time you're thinking about the email, the dishes, the thing somebody said at lunch. Now put a word on each breath. Not shouted, not even spoken. Just there, like a passenger. Many Sikhs do exactly this with one word, the word the Sikh code of conduct calls the Gurmantar. They split it in two. The first half rides in. The second half rides out. That's today.
screen: `BREATHS NOBODY NOTICES.` → `A WORD RIDING EACH ONE.` → `ONE WORD, SPLIT IN TWO.`

segments.voice: The word is Waheguru. You've met it already on this path: it's the word Sikhs call the Gurmantar, the Guru's own word for remembering God. Let's open it. Wahe is an exclamation of wonder. It's close to wow, the sound you make when a view stops you on a hill road. Guru means the teacher, the guide. So Waheguru is something like wonderful Teacher, a cry of wonder at the Divine. Now the breath. Many Sikhs practice simran by letting Wahe rise on the in-breath and Guru fall on the out-breath. Wahe in. Guru out. The in-breath is the wonder, taking in. The out-breath is the Guru, letting go into trust. It's slow, and it's silent, or nearly so. Some people say it quietly on the lips. Some only in the mind. Others don't split the word at all and repeat the whole of Waheguru aloud, in rhythm, or sing it in kirtan with the sangat. Sikh teachers and groups differ on the details, and the Guru Granth Sahib doesn't lay down a breathing method. What the hymns do say, over and over, is that a breath without the Name is wasted, and a breath with it is precious. So the breath is not a trick. It's a clock you already carry, ticking whether you mean it to or not. Simran on the breath simply asks that some of them remember where they came from.
screen: `WAHE — A CRY OF WONDER.` · `GURU — THE TEACHER, THE GUIDE.` · `WAHE IN, GURU OUT.` · `A CLOCK YOU ALREADY CARRY.` · then, large: `WAHEGURU.`

segments.voice: Let's try ten breaths this way. Sit comfortably. Let the breath find its own speed. On the next in-breath, think Wahe, slowly, the whole length of the breath. On the out-breath, think Guru, all the way to the end. That's one. Keep going, and count on your fingers if it helps. If you're here to learn rather than to pray, just listen to how the two halves feel different. After ten, let the words go and keep breathing. The bell holds the time.
Wahe in. The first half of Waheguru, the wonder, riding on the in-breath. Guru rides out.
Your line: wahe in, guru out. Today, pick one thing you do many times, like opening a door or unlocking your phone, and give it one breath this way. Day one hundred twenty-one.

122.title: Satnam on the breath
122.hook: Sat on the inhale, Nam on the exhale
122.howItsDone: Satnam, from the opening line of the Guru Granth Sahib, is repeated in simran by some Sikhs, sometimes with Sat on the in-breath and Nam on the out-breath, and sometimes together with Waheguru.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Waheguru split across the breath. Your line was wahe in, guru out. Which ordinary moment did you give one breath to? Day one hundred twenty-two.

The people you love tend to have more than one name. The full name on the birth certificate. The nickname. The name only you use. Each one holds something different. The Guru Granth Sahib is like that about God. It uses many names, from many languages: Hari, Ram, Allah, Gobind, Prabhu, Kartar. But right at the very start of the book, in its first line, there's a name that isn't really a name at all. It's a description. Two syllables, and it fits a breath exactly.
screen: `MANY NAMES FOR ONE YOU LOVE.` → `DOZENS OF NAMES FOR GOD.` → `ONE THAT FITS A BREATH.`

segments.voice: The Guru Granth Sahib opens with the Mul Mantar, the root verse. It begins with Ik Onkar, there is one God. And the very next word is Satnam. Sat means true, real, what lasts. Nam means name. So Satnam is the true name, or better, the one whose name is truth. Here's the quiet surprise. Guru Nanak doesn't give God a proper name at this point. He gives a quality. Right after saying God is one, the text says God is real. Not a rumor, not a mood. True. Sikhs don't treat Satnam as a different God or a secret password. It's a way of saying the same One, by what never changes. That's why it works so well as simran. Sat on the in-breath: the real, coming in. Nam on the out-breath: the name, going out into the day. Many Sikhs use Waheguru for simran, since that's the Gurmantar, and some also breathe with Satnam, or say Satnam Waheguru together. Practices differ from sangat to sangat, and both words appear in the Guru Granth Sahib. You may have heard Satnam used as a greeting too, or heard it in yoga classes in the West. The everyday Sikh greeting is something else, Sat Sri Akal, but the word sat is in there as well. Truth keeps turning up. Guru Nanak says elsewhere in the Granth that truth is high, but higher still is truthful living. Satnam on the breath starts there: one real thing, noticed, again and again.

segments.voice: Ten breaths again, with the new word. Let your shoulders drop. On the in-breath, think Sat, and let it last as long as the breath does. On the out-breath, think Nam, all the way out. If you pray, you can let it be prayer. If you're here to learn, try hearing it as a plain word: true, name. Notice whether it feels different from yesterday's Wahe and Guru. Then just breathe. The bell holds the time.
Satnam on the breath. Sat is true, Nam is name: the one whose name is truth, right after Ik Onkar at the opening of the Guru Granth Sahib.
Your line: true name, breathing. Today, when something you hear feels false or fake, take one Satnam breath before you answer. Day one hundred twenty-two.

123.title: When the mind runs off
123.hook: the hymns often call the mind restless; the practice is only to come back
123.howItsDone: Sikh teachers describe the wandering mind as the normal condition the hymns address, and simran as gently returning attention to the Name each time it drifts.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Satnam on the breath: Sat on the in-breath, Nam on the out. Your line was true name, breathing. And be honest: how many of those ten breaths did you actually stay with? Day one hundred twenty-three.

Here's what usually happens. You sit down. You start the breath and the word. Wahe, Guru. Wahe, Guru. On the third breath you remember you never answered your sister's message. On the fourth you're planning dinner. By the sixth you're replaying an argument from 2019, and you've won it this time. Then, suddenly, you notice. Oh. I was supposed to be doing something. It's easy to read that moment as failure. The Gurus saw it very differently.
screen: `THE THIRD BREATH: A MESSAGE.` → `THE SIXTH: AN OLD ARGUMENT.` → `OH. I WANDERED.`

segments.voice: In Punjabi the mind is man, and the hymns of the Guru Granth Sahib talk to it constantly, almost like a friend who won't sit still. They describe it running in all ten directions, chasing one thing after another, never staying in one place. The Gurus aren't surprised by this. They expect it. That's the first comfort: a wandering mind is not a sign you're doing it wrong. It's the normal weather the hymns are written for. The second thing is how the Gurus speak to the mind. Not only with scolding. Guru Amar Das addresses it with astonishing tenderness. In paraphrase: O my mind, you are the very form of divine light; know where you came from. Think about that. The restless thing that ran off to your 2019 argument is, in this line, made of light. It isn't the enemy. It's something that forgot its home. So the practice is not to chain the mind down. It's only to come back. You notice you've wandered, and that noticing is itself the moment of simran. Then you return to the next breath, and the word, without a lecture. If it wanders again in ten seconds, you come back again. A hundred times is fine. One way to picture it: simran is less like building a wall and more like calling a child home at dusk. You don't shout at the child for playing. You're just glad when they're back at the door.
screen: `MAN — THE MIND, RUNNING TEN WAYS.` · `THE GURUS EXPECT IT.` · `O MIND, YOU ARE FORMED OF LIGHT.` · `NOTICING IS THE SIMRAN.` · then, large: `COME BACK.`

segments.voice: Let's practice wandering, on purpose. Start with the breath and whichever word you like, Waheguru or Satnam, or just the breath if you'd rather. Your mind will run off. When it does, notice where it went, name it in one word, like work or food or worry, and come back to the next breath. Kindly, the way you'd welcome that child home. See if you can come back three times. The bell holds the time.
When the mind runs off. The hymns expect it to. The practice is not to stop it running, only to notice and come back.
screen: `WHEN THE MIND RUNS OFF — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: come back. Today, every time you catch yourself drifting, in a meeting or a line or a conversation, don't scold. Just come back, one breath. Day one hundred twenty-three.

124.title: The early hours
124.hook: the ambrosial hours before dawn, praised in Japji's fourth pauri
124.howItsDone: Many Sikhs rise in the amrit vela, the hours before dawn, to bathe, recite the morning banis and do simran before the day's work begins.

segments.voice: Yesterday, when the mind runs off. Your line was come back. How many times did you catch yourself drifting, and did you manage to come back without a scolding? Day one hundred twenty-four.
screen: `WHEN THE MIND RUNS OFF — COME BACK.`

segments.voice: There's an hour most of us only meet by accident. The flight that leaves at six. The baby who won't settle. The night you couldn't sleep and finally gave up and made tea. The house is silent. No messages are coming in, because everyone you know is asleep. Even the birds haven't started. It feels strange, a little lonely, and oddly clean. Sikhs have a name for that hour, and they don't treat it as an accident. They treat it as a gift, and some Sikhs set an alarm for it.
screen: `THE SIX O'CLOCK FLIGHT.` → `A SILENT HOUSE, NO MESSAGES.` → `AN HOUR WITH A NAME.`

segments.voice: The name is amrit vela. Vela means time, or hour. Amrit is nectar, the drink of immortality in old Indian stories, the thing that makes life deathless. So amrit vela is the nectar hour, often translated the ambrosial hour. It's the last watch of the night, before dawn. The text gives no clock time for it. It comes from Japji, Guru Nanak's morning hymn, the same fourth pauri where you met nadar, grace, on day one hundred eighteen. In that pauri, the fourth stanza, he asks what we can offer to the One who gives everything, and answers: in the ambrosial hours, contemplate the true Name and its greatness. That's the whole instruction. No ritual. No list. Just the Name, in the early hour. Later, Guru Ram Das describes a Sikh's day, in paraphrase: one who calls himself a Sikh of the true Guru rises early and meditates on the Name, bathes, and keeps remembering through the day. Why so early? Sikh writers give a few reasons. The mind is quieter before the world starts pulling on it. The day hasn't made any claims yet, so the first thing it hears is the Name. And there's something honest about giving up a little sleep: it costs something. In many Sikh homes and gurdwaras the day really does begin this way, with Nitnem and simran in the dark, and at the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar the Guru Granth Sahib is brought out in procession before dawn. Nobody has to become a monk to try it. Five minutes counts.
screen: `AMRIT — NECTAR. VELA — HOUR.` · `JAPJI'S FOURTH PAURI.` · `THE NAME, IN THE EARLY HOUR.` · `IT COSTS A LITTLE SLEEP.` · then, large: `AMRIT VELA.`

segments.voice: Today's practice has two parts. First, right now: pick up your phone or picture your alarm, and set it five minutes earlier for tomorrow. Just five. Then close your eyes and imagine that extra five minutes: the dark room, the quiet, the breath, and, if you pray, a word like Waheguru, before anything else gets in. If you're here to learn, imagine simply sitting with the silence. Stay with that picture now. The bell holds the time.
Amrit vela. The nectar hour before dawn, praised in Japji's fourth pauri as the time to remember the true Name.
Your line: the early hour. Tomorrow, when that alarm goes five minutes early, don't reach for the phone first. Give the quiet its five minutes. Day one hundred twenty-four.

125.title: A string of beads
125.hook: some keep count of simran on a string of beads
125.howItsDone: Some Sikhs use a mala, often of wool or iron beads, to count repetitions of Waheguru during simran; many others do simran without one, and the Sikh code of conduct does not require it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, amrit vela, the nectar hour before dawn. Your line was the early hour. Did the alarm go five minutes early, and what did you do with them? Day one hundred twenty-five.

Watch the hands of an older Sikh man sitting at the back of a gurdwara, or a grandmother on a bus in Punjab. Sometimes you'll see a small loop of beads moving through the fingers, one at a time, while the lips move very slightly. No book open. No phone. Just thumb, bead, thumb, bead. Your grandparents may have done this too, in whatever tradition they came from: people all over the world have found that hands like having something to hold while the heart remembers. Today, the Sikh string of beads.
screen: `A LOOP OF BEADS IN THE FINGERS.` → `THUMB, BEAD, THUMB, BEAD.` → `HANDS THAT HELP THE HEART.`

segments.voice: It's called a mala, which simply means a garland or a string. A Sikh mala is often made of wool, or sometimes of iron or steel beads, and many have one hundred and eight beads, though smaller ones are common too. Some Nihang Sikhs, the traditional warrior order in blue, wear large malas around the neck or wrist. The use is simple. With each bead, the one repeating says the Name once, usually Waheguru, and moves on. The mala keeps count so the mind doesn't have to, and it gives restless fingers something to do. Now, here's what makes the Sikh view of beads interesting. The Guru Granth Sahib is honest that beads on their own do nothing. The Gurus and the saints in the Granth were sharp about outward show: counting beads for others to see while the heart is elsewhere. Kabir, one of the saints whose verses are in the Granth, turns the whole idea around. In paraphrase, he says: my mala is my tongue, and the Name of the Lord is strung on it. The real string of beads is inside. So Sikhs hold the mala lightly. Many use one gladly as a help. Many never use one at all and count nothing, and the Sikh code of conduct doesn't require it. Both are at home in the gurdwara. The point is never the count. The point is that each bead is one more moment of remembering, and a hundred and eight small moments add up to something.
screen: `MALA — A GARLAND, A STRING.` · `ONE BEAD, ONE NAME.` · `BEADS ALONE DO NOTHING.` · `MY MALA IS MY TONGUE.` · then, large: `BEAD BY BEAD.`

segments.voice: No beads needed. Use your fingers. Touch your thumb to each finger segment in turn: three segments on four fingers is twelve. Go around your hand, then around again, and a bit more, for twenty-seven, a quarter of a full mala. With each touch, say one word silently: Waheguru, if you pray, or simply your breath if you'd rather. Don't worry if you lose count. Start again wherever you are. The bell holds the time.
Mala. A garland, a string of beads, often a hundred and eight, that some Sikhs use to count the Name.
Your line: bead by bead. Today, pick something you touch often, a ring, a key, a button, and let each touch be one small remembering. Day one hundred twenty-five.

126.title: Simran while working
126.hook: the Name can run quietly underneath ordinary work
126.carry: hands at work, heart at home
126.howItsDone: Many Sikhs keep up simran through the working day, quietly repeating Waheguru, listening to kirtan while they work, or pausing for a breath of remembering between tasks.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mala, a string of beads. Your line was bead by bead. And a week on the breath is nearly done: naam simran, Wahe in, Satnam, coming back, the early hour, the beads. Which one stuck? Day one hundred twenty-six.
screen: `BREATH · WAHEGURU · SATNAM · COME BACK · AMRIT VELA · MALA.`

segments.voice: Here's the problem with everything we've done this week. You can't sit with your eyes closed all day. There's a job. There are kids, a commute, a sink full of dishes, a shift that starts at seven. If remembering God only happens in the quiet corner before dawn, then most of the day is left out. The Sikh Gurus were never monks. They farmed, traded, married and ran communities. So they had to answer this. Their answer is in a small, funny conversation between two saints.
screen: `YOU CAN'T SIT ALL DAY.` → `THE GURUS WERE NEVER MONKS.` → `A CONVERSATION BETWEEN TWO SAINTS.`

segments.voice: Among the short verses of Kabir in the Guru Granth Sahib, there's an exchange between two earlier saints of India, Trilochan and Namdev. Namdev was a cloth printer by trade, working with dyes all day. Trilochan teases him, in paraphrase: Namdev, you've been caught by the world. Why are you busy printing calico? Why not fix your mind on the Lord? And Namdev answers, in paraphrase: with your mouth, keep the Lord's Name; with your hands and feet, do all your work; keep your consciousness with the Immaculate One. That's it. The work doesn't stop. The remembering doesn't stop. One runs underneath the other, like a song you hum while you cook. This fits the whole Sikh way of life. The three pillars Sikhs trace to Guru Nanak, you've met them already: naam japo, remember the Name; kirat karo, earn an honest living; vand chhako, share. They sit side by side. Honest work isn't a distraction from the spiritual life. For Sikhs, it's part of it. So what does simran while working look like? For some, a quiet Waheguru under the breath while stacking shelves or driving. For others, a recording of kirtan playing while they work. For others, a single breath of remembering each time a task begins or ends. The hymns hold up remembering with every breath; in a working day, the picture is more like a home the heart can return to all day, while the hands stay busy. The hands are at work. The heart knows where home is.
screen: `TRILOCHAN TEASES NAMDEV.` · `HANDS AND FEET DO THE WORK.` · `REMEMBER, WORK, SHARE.` · `THE NAME RUNS UNDERNEATH.` · then, large: `HANDS AT WORK, HEART AT HOME.`

segments.voice: Today, simran while walking. If you can, stand up and walk slowly: around the room, down a hallway, or just in place. Let each step land with a word. Left foot, Wahe. Right foot, Guru. Or, if you'd rather, left foot, in-breath, right foot, out. Keep your eyes open. You're still in the world, doing something ordinary, and the remembering is running underneath it. When the mind runs off, come back. The bell holds the time.
Simran while working. The Name running quietly underneath ordinary work, as Namdev said: hands and feet at work, the heart with the One.
Your line: hands at work, heart at home. Today, choose one task, the dishes, a spreadsheet, a drive, and let a quiet word run under it for the first minute. Day one hundred twenty-six.
